newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-FOCUS-Already on a roll, zinc seen higher yet.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-FOCUS-Already on a roll, zinc seen higher yet.

text.p: Zinc prices, which are trading near four-and-a-half year highs, are on a roll and poised to go higher as demand for the metal outpaces supplies, analysts and producers said on Friday.
"We've liked zinc for over a year now," Macquarie Bank Ltd analyst Jim Lennon said.

Lennon told a Macquarie Bank zinc industry symposium here that zinc would average at least 56 U.S. cents a pound this year and climb to 65 cents in 1998 on the back of higher consumption and the influnece of hedge funds on the price.
The 1996 average price was 46 cents a pound.
Zinc ended afternoon trading on Thursday at US$1,280 a tonne or 58 cents a pound.
"We've been forecasting a growth rate of 2.7 percent in 1997 and 3.1 percent in 1998," Lennon said.

Meanwhile, spot zinc premiums in the U.S. for Special High Grade-brand zinc are poised to climb by a few cents to around eight or nine cents a pound due to an emerging supply pinch, general manager of marketing for Savage Resource Ltd, which operates the Savage Zinc Co of the U.S. said.
This compares with long-term contract premiums of closer to five or six cents a pound over the LME price, Boyer said.
Little SGH zinc existed in LME warehouses beyond that produced by Spanish zinc company Asturiana de Zinc SA, much of which was now controlled by a Swiss trading company.
Late last year, Asturiana said it had gradually liquidated its zinc position on the LME through Glencore International in 1996.
U.S. steel mills look to purchase SHG zinc, Boyer said.
Less pricy high grade-type zinc usually trades at a discount of four to five cents a pound to the LME, he said.
Boyer said he sees the current contango in the market narrowing and possiblly a backwardation eventually emerging as nearby supplies tightness.
Boyer said the U.S. was destinmed to remain a net importer of large quantities of zinc, most of which would come from Canada.
"There is no question the U.S. will be a major importer of metal for years to come," Boyer told the symposium.
Boyer said a A$10 million study into expanding Savage's 105,000-tonnes-a-year zinc refinery in Clarksville, Tenn by 175,000 tonnes would be completed by the end of 1997.
Robust demand for zinc reflected in healthy market premiums, relatively cheap labour and energy and U.S. dollar-denominated sales all supported the case for an expansion, Boyer said.
Growth in consumption of zinc in the U.S. will lift consumption to 1.32 million in 1998 from a forecast 1.3 million this year, Savage figures show.
This year scope existed for imports to the U.S. of 888,00 tonnes, Savage figures show.
-- James Regan Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
